paper_a.title: Testing Graph Properties with the Container Method

paper_b.title: A container theorem for general digraphs with forbidden subdigraphs

metadata.description: Both papers deploy the (graph/hypergraph) container method but at different layers of the toolchain. Paper A (Blais-Seth) USES container-style covering lemmas, custom-built directly via a Kleitman-Winston-flavored greedy procedure, to obtain sample-complexity upper bounds for property testing of $\rho$-Clique/IndepSet and $k$-Colorability. Paper B (Liu) PROVES a new container theorem for general digraphs (extending KOTZ's oriented-graph version) by reducing to the Saxton-Thomason hypergraph container theorem via an auxiliary $r$-uniform hypergraph $\mathcal{D}(N,H)$. The shared technical core is the container/fingerprint covering paradigm; the two papers occupy the consumer vs. producer roles of that paradigm and target distinct problems (property testing vs. extremal/counting), making the pair a clean SM (same method) instance rather than EXT or AP.

matches.explanation: Both sides are the central 'container theorem' statements of their respective papers. Paper A's Graph Container Lemmas I and II (for $\rho$-IndepSet and $k$-colorability respectively) assert the existence of fingerprint families $\mathcal{F}$ and container maps $\mathcal{C}$ such that every large independent / $k$-colorable substructure $U$ satisfies $F\subseteq U\subseteq\mathcal{C}(F)$ for some $F\in\mathcal{F}$, with explicit fingerprint-size and container-size bounds tuned to property testing. Paper B's Main Theorem is the digraph analogue of KOTZ-style container theorems: every $H$-free digraph is contained in some $G\in\mathcal{C}$ with $\le \eps N^h$ copies of $H$, $e_a(G)\le\mathrm{ex}_a(N,H)+\eps N^2$, and $\log|\mathcal{C}|\le c N^{2-1/m(H)}\log N$. Same covering-by-containers conclusion; different host structure (graph vs. digraph) and different downstream targets (sample bounds vs. extremal counts), hence analogous rather than exact.

Paper A's container lemmas play the same role as the cited KOTZ container theorem (TP441.1) in paper B, namely a 'container theorem' tailored to the host class. KOTZ is for $H$-free oriented graphs; the Blais-Seth lemmas are for graphs $\eps$-far from $\rho$-IndepSet / $k$-colorable. Both produce a small fingerprint-indexed cover of the structures of interest with quantitative bounds on container size; the surface conclusions differ (covering count $\log|\mathcal{C}|\le c N^{2-1/m(H)}\log N$ vs. cardinality bounds tied to $\rho,k,\eps$) because the two papers extract different consequences. Confidence medium because the cross-paper alignment is conceptual (same method) rather than literal.

Both papers construct the technical machinery that drives the container conclusion. Paper A builds it directly: a Kleitman-Winston greedy algorithm (AP432.1) generating fingerprint/container sequences (DP432.7), with structural properties (closure PrP432.1, max-degree bound PrP432.2, monotone chain EP432.1). Paper B builds it indirectly: an auxiliary $r$-uniform hypergraph $\mathcal{D}(N,H)$ (DP441.5) whose independent sets correspond to $H$-free digraphs, plus the codegree estimate (LP441.1) needed to invoke Saxton-Thomason. These are 'container construction kits' on either side: both reduce the existence of a small fingerprint cover to a structural/degree property of an auxiliary object. Paper B outsources the actual container construction to TP441.2; paper A inlines it. Cluster correspondence on each side.

These are the workhorse counting/structural lemmas inside each container construction. Paper A's Container Shrinking Lemma (LP432.3), Graph Container Lemma I 'alternative formulation' (LP432.4), and Graph Container Lemma II 'alternative formulation' (LP432.5) bound how fast the greedy procedure shrinks the container in the IndepSet and $k$-colorable settings respectively, controlling fingerprint size and container density via $\eps$-farness. Paper B's degree estimate (LP441.1) bounds the codegree function $\delta(\mathcal{D}(N,H),\tau)$ so that Saxton-Thomason applies. Both feed a quantitative bound about the auxiliary structure into the master container theorem; both rely on a density/maximum-subgraph argument ($m(H)$ on the digraph side; the max-degree-bound proposition on the graph side). Medium confidence: the role is parallel but the bookkeeping is quite different.

Paper-A-specific proofs of the container closure property (PrP432.1) and container max-degree bound (PrP432.2). These are bookkeeping facts about the greedy fingerprint/container construction that has no analogue on the paper-B side, where containers are obtained as a black-box from Saxton-Thomason.

Both proofs are the central density/structural argument inside their respective container constructions. Paper A's PP432.3 proves the Container Shrinking Lemma by case analysis (high-degree vertex vs. dense $G[C_t\setminus C]$) using $\eps$-farness. Paper B's PP441.1 proves the codegree estimate for $\mathcal{D}(N,H)$ via a five-step counting argument culminating in the $m(H)$-tuned bound. Both are the 'do the actual estimate' proof that feeds the higher-level container statement; both use the host structure ($\eps$-farness vs. Condition A and $m(H)$) to extract the needed density bound. Confidence medium because the bookkeeping is quite different.
Paper-A-specific proof of the cited Chernoff-for-hypergeometric bound (LP432.6). No analogue on the paper-B side.

Paper A's proofs of the precise Theorems 1 and 2 are sampling/concentration-style soundness arguments (union-bound over fingerprints, apply Chernoff to conditional containment). The closest paper-B analogue is the corollary on counting $H$-free digraphs (CP441.1), which trivially follows from the main theorem by summing $2^{e(G)}$ over the container collection -- but paper B does not extract this as a separate proof node, so the structural counterpart is absent. Listed as none with medium confidence since one could argue the corollary's implicit proof plays the parallel role.

Both papers define the basic complexity/extremal quantity their main theorem bounds. Paper A defines $\eps$-far from a property, the canonical $\eps$-tester, and sample complexity $\mathcal{S}_\Pi(n,\eps)$ -- the quantity Theorems 1-2 upper-bound. Paper B defines $\mathrm{ex}_a(n,H)$, the Turan-type extremal weighted size that the container theorem certifies up to $\eps N^2$. The match is loose: both are 'the headline parameter our theorem controls', but the underlying mathematics (statistical-query lower-envelope vs. extremal-graph-theoretic max) is quite different. Confidence low.

Cited Chernoff/hypergeometric bound is paper-A-specific machinery for the property-testing soundness analysis; paper B has no analogue (it does not perform any random-sampling concentration argument). Skipped per origin filtering rules but worth flagging as a real asymmetry: paper A's pipeline ends in a sampling/concentration argument (Theorem 1-2), whereas paper B's pipeline ends in a counting argument (Corollary 1).

These are the 'downstream applications' that justify each paper's container machinery. Paper A's Theorems 1, 1', 2, and their precise versions give sample-complexity upper bounds for testing $\rho$-Clique, Densest-$k$-Subgraph, and $k$-colorability. Paper B's Corollary derives the asymptotic count of $H$-free digraphs $f^*(n,H) = 2^{\mathrm{ex}_2(n,H)+o(n^2)}$. In both cases the container theorem feeds into a union-bound-style argument that yields the headline quantitative conclusion of the paper. The applications themselves are not analogous (testing vs. counting), but they are functionally parallel within their respective container-method pipelines. Medium confidence because the analogy is at the architectural level only.

Each side's main proofs of their container statement. Paper A's PP432.5 and PP432.7 prove Lemmas I and II by constructing $\mathcal{F}$ from fingerprints of large independent sets / $k$-partitions and $\mathcal{C}(F)$ from greedy containers, with PP432.4 and PP432.6 proving the alternative formulations needed as inputs. Paper B's PP441.2 proves the main container theorem by checking the Saxton-Thomason hypotheses via Lemma 3.1 and then translating containers in $\mathcal{D}(N,H)$ back to digraphs $G_C$. Both proofs share the 'reduce to a container statement on an auxiliary structure, then translate back' template, but paper A executes it from scratch while paper B reduces to Saxton-Thomason as a black box; hence analogous rather than exact, with medium confidence.

Composite L2 entry attached to the main-theorem proofs above. The inner step DAGs differ in interesting ways: paper A's proof of LP432.4 (PSP432.6-PSP432.9) iterates the Container Shrinking Lemma to bound the number of greedy rounds before $G[C_t]$ becomes $\eps n^2/4$-sparse -- the iteration is the heart of the construction. Paper B's main-theorem proof (PSP441.7-PSP441.11) is a thin orchestration layer over the codegree lemma (3.1) and Saxton-Thomason (2.1), with the actual heavy lifting done in Lemma 3.1's separate proof PP441.1 / PSP441.1-6. So the steps are 'iteratively shrink containers' on the A side vs. 'plug numbers into a black-box' on the B side -- a structural asymmetry that itself is informative (paper B inherits the iteration implicit in Saxton-Thomason). Confidence low because the step-level alignment is rough.

Paper A's two canonical testers (sample $s$ vertices and accept iff $G[S]$ has the property) are paper-original algorithms with no counterpart in paper B. Paper B is purely structural/extremal: it does not propose an algorithm, only an existence statement about a container collection $\mathcal{C}$. The asymmetry reflects the paper-A-specific algorithmic application of containers.

Paper A's specific tested properties ($\rho$-Clique, $\rho$-IndepSet, $k$-Colorable) are paper-A-specific instances. Paper B works at the level of an arbitrary digraph $H$ satisfying Condition A, parametrically. The 'forbidden subdigraph $H$' in paper B is the abstract analogue of these specific properties, but no individual node in paper B singles out a particular $H$.

Paper A's headline problems are property-testing decision problems. Paper B has no problem-typed node on the testing side; its concerns are extremal-graph-theoretic. Listed as none for completeness on the paper-A paper-origin Level-1 nodes.
Open question about the optimality of $\tilde{O}(k/\eps)$ for $k$-colorability testing -- paper-A-specific testing-side question with no paper-B counterpart.

Both open problems ask: 'for which class of objects does the container method give optimal bounds?'. Paper A asks for the largest class of graph/hypergraph properties admitting tight property-testing bounds via containers. Paper B asks for the characterisation of digraphs $H$ admitting a container theorem (suggesting $m(H)$ or 2-cycle-multiplicity bounds). Same meta-question (extending the reach of the container method) on different downstream domains (testing vs. extremal counting) -- a clean instance of the SM relationship at the open-problem level.

Cited prior bounds on $\rho$-Clique and $k$-colorability testing (GGR98, FLS04, AK02, Sohler12). Paper-A-specific external-origin context for the testing problem; paper B has no analogue cited works since its application domain is different. Listed as none for transparency, though external-origin nodes do not strictly require none entries.

Paper B's basic digraph definitions (weighted size $e_a$, 2-cycle, codegree function $\delta(\mathcal{H},\tau)$) are paper-B-specific. Paper A operates in undirected graph land throughout; there is no notion of weighted edge count, 2-cycle, or codegree-of-hypergraph machinery on the paper-A side. The codegree function in particular is a Saxton-Thomason artefact paper B inherits and that paper A does not need (paper A's iteration is self-contained).

Paper B's Condition A (sparsity assumption $e(H')/v(H')\le a/2$) and density parameter $m(H)$ are paper-B-specific extremal-graph-theoretic devices. Paper A neither requires nor produces an analogous host-graph density assumption; its hypotheses are simply '$G$ is $\eps$-far from $\Pi$'. The asymmetry highlights what makes paper B a method-extension paper (proving a theorem) versus paper A a method-deployment paper (using containers).

Saxton-Thomason hypergraph container theorem. Paper B treats this as an external black-box. Paper A does not invoke Saxton-Thomason; it constructs containers from scratch via Kleitman-Winston. This non-match is precisely the central methodological difference between the two papers and a strong signal that the relationship is SM (same method family, different layers / different ways of obtaining the container guarantee).

Paper B's worked examples ($DK_3$ counterexample at $a=2$; $a=4$ allowing 2-cycles) sharpen Condition A. Paper A has no analogous discussion since it does not need a host-graph density condition. Skipped per the compactness rule for examples/remarks, but listed here for completeness given the prominence of $DK_3$ in paper B's framing.
